cited_works.title: Poisson pre-processing of nonstationary photonic signals: Signals with equality between mean and variance
cited_works.abstract: Photonic signals are broadly exploited in communication and sensing and they typically exhibit Poisson-like statistics. In a common scenario where the intensity of the photonic signals is low and one needs to remove a nonstationary trend of the signals for any further analysis, one faces an obstacle: due to the dependence between the mean and variance typical for a Poisson-like process, information about the trend remains in the variance even after the trend has been subtracted, possibly yielding artifactual results in further analyses. Commonly available detrending or normalizing methods cannot cope with this issue. To alleviate this issue we developed a suitable pre-processing method for the signals that originate from a Poisson-like process. In this paper, a Poisson pre-processing method for nonstationary time series with Poisson distribution is developed and tested on computer-generated model data and experimental data of chemiluminescence from human neutrophils and mung seeds. The presented method transforms a nonstationary Poisson signal into a stationary signal with a Poisson distribution while preserving the type of photocount distribution and phase-space structure of the signal. The importance of the suggested pre-processing method is shown in Fano factor and Hurst exponent analysis of both computer-generated model signals and experimental photonic signals. It is demonstrated that our pre-processing method is superior to standard detrending-based methods whenever further signal analysis is sensitive to variance of the signal.

cited_works.title: Short-time fractal analysis of biological autoluminescence
cited_works.abstract: Biological systems manifest continuous weak autoluminescence, which is present even in the absence of external stimuli. Since this autoluminescence arises from internal metabolic and physiological processes, several works suggested that it could carry information in the time series of the detected photon counts. However, there is little experimental work which would show any difference of this signal from random Poisson noise and some works were prone to artifacts due to lacking or improper reference signals. Here we apply rigorous statistical methods and advanced reference signals to test the hypothesis whether time series of autoluminescence from germinating mung beans display any intrinsic correlations. Utilizing the fractional Brownian bridge that employs short samples of time series in the method kernel, we suggest that the detected autoluminescence signal from mung beans is not totally random, but it seems to involve a process with a negative memory. Our results contribute to the development of the rigorous methodology of signal analysis of photonic biosignals.

statement: A sealed, chemically defined luminescent transfer standard circulated among independent UPE laboratories will be reported in absolute units (photons s-1 into 4 pi, 400-650 nm) with a between-laboratory log10 standard deviation at least three times smaller than the between-laboratory log10 standard deviation obtained by the same laboratories on a common biological sample, demonstrating that the field's non-comparability is dominated by the calibration chain rather than by biological variance.

scope.population: At least five independent laboratories that routinely publish UPE measurements, each using its own detector and its own current calibration practice
scope.condition: Two artefacts circulated in a round-robin: (a) a sealed chemical reference emitter - luminol at defined concentration/pH, and a Fe(II)/H2O2 Fenton cell in defined buffer - in a standardised cuvette and holder; (b) a standardised biological sample - a defined mass of Vigna radiata seeds imbibed under a fixed protocol
scope.comparator: The same laboratories' raw instrument-native reports (counts/s or relative light units) for both artefacts, and a light-tight blank of identical geometry
scope.outcome: Absolute emission rate in photons s-1 (4 pi, 400-650 nm) reported by each laboratory for each artefact, with each laboratory's declared uncertainty budget

null_hypothesis: Between-laboratory agreement on the chemical transfer standard is no better than on the biological sample (log10 SD ratio < 3), meaning radiometric calibration is not the dominant source of the field's disagreement and standardisation of the detection chain alone will not deliver comparability.
estimand: Ratio R = SD_log10(absolute rate, biological sample) / SD_log10(absolute rate, chemical standard), across laboratories; secondary estimand: the fraction of participating laboratories able to report an absolute rate at all.
proposed_experiment: Build two sealed transfer artefacts (a luminol cell and a Fe(II)/H2O2 Fenton cell, both in an identical quartz cuvette and light-tight holder, with a certified stable output over the circulation window) plus a matched dark blank, and ship them sequentially to >=5 UPE laboratories with a fixed measurement protocol but no prescribed calibration method. Each laboratory returns raw counts, its stated conversion to photons s-1 (4 pi, 400-650 nm), and its uncertainty budget. Repeat with a standardised mung-bean germination sample prepared identically at each site. Compute the two between-laboratory log10 SDs and their ratio. Pre-register R >= 3 as support and R < 3 as refutation. Anchor the chain to an SI-traceable absolute detector efficiency at one node using SPDC correlated-pair (Klyshko) calibration.

rationale.step: Given by the seed brief: the field states that luminescence-detection papers rarely report light signals in absolute photon numbers and never report detection limits in units of photon emission rate density, precluding any direct sensitivity comparison; and that UPE remains a technical curiosity rather than a reliable biomarker in the absence of standardization.

Chemical luminescence standards are already the accepted way to calibrate a photon-counting detector in this literature: the luminol standard is described as the easiest way to calibrate the PMT of a light-detection device, and absolute chemiluminescence intensities have been estimated by comparison against the luminol standard.

A precedent exists in this corpus for converting a biological UPE measurement to absolute units via a calibrated light source, and that conversion was decisive: absolute bio-emission intensity from frog and sterlet retinas was found to be at least 100x lower than required to produce discrete rod dark noise, which rejected a standing hypothesis. Absolute units, not counts, carried the inferential weight.

Candidate chemical emitters at the right intensity scale are demonstrated in the corpus: non-catalytic disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide in pure water produces detectable ultraweak luminescence, and Fenton-reagent-initiated oxidation produces a dose-dependent autoluminescence signal in yeast culture, so a chemically defined cell can be tuned to the UPE flux regime rather than the bright-chemiluminescence regime.

The failure mode the round-robin targets is documented in the neighbouring low-light field: a systematic review of 74 photobiomodulation papers found 73% reported no information on how light was measured and relied on manufacturer-stated values, with power missing in 41%, beam area in 40%, irradiance in 43% and radiant energy in 74% - and the authors' remedy is a mandatory ten-parameter reporting list. The same remedy is testable in UPE by round-robin.

That UPE laboratories currently publish in non-convertible instrument-native units is directly observable in the corpus: recent measurement papers report emission solely as relative light units from a commercial luminometer, with the RLU asserted to indicate photons per second per square centimetre but no conversion factor, QE curve or collection geometry given.

Computation of the expected effect size. The detected rate is C = Phi * A_eff * g * eta_bar * T, where g is the geometric collection factor, eta_bar the band-averaged quantum efficiency, T the optical transmission and A_eff the emitting area. Reported human-surface UPE spans 1-1000 photons s-1 cm-2 in one source and 10-10^3 in another, i.e. three decades. If g, eta_bar and T each carry an unreported factor-of-3 uncertainty, their product spans 27x (1.4 decades) - about half the observed literature spread - so the round-robin has the dynamic range to separate the metrological from the biological component.

cited_works.title: Chemi- and Bioluminescence of Cyclic Peroxides
cited_works.abstract: Bioluminescence is a phenomenon that has fascinated mankind for centuries. Today the phenomenon and its sibling, chemiluminescence, have impacted society with a number of useful applications in fields like analytical chemistry and medicine, just to mention two. In this review, a molecular-orbital perspective is adopted to explain the chemistry behind chemiexcitation in both chemi- and bioluminescence. First, the uncatalyzed thermal dissociation of 1,2-dioxetane is presented and analyzed to explain, for example, the preference for triplet excited product states and increased yield with larger nonreactive substituents. The catalyzed fragmentation reaction and related details are then exemplified with substituted 1,2-dioxetanone species. In particular, the preference for singlet excited product states in that case is explained. The review also examines the diversity of specific solutions both in Nature and in artificial systems and the difficulties in identifying the emitting species and unraveling the color modulation process. The related subject of excited-state chemistry without light absorption is finally discussed. The content of this review should be an inspiration to human design of new molecular systems expressing unique light-emitting properties. An appendix describing the state-of-the-art experimental and theoretical methods used to study the phenomena serves as a complement.

cited_works.title: CHEMILUMINESCENCE IN THE PHOTOOXIDATION OF HUMIC ACIDS*
cited_works.abstract: Abstract— Photo‐irradiation of aqueous basic solutions of soil humic acids and synthetic melanins with UV and visible light (Λ > 320 nm) under oxygen or nitrogen atmospheres generates electronic exicted states and radicals. These processes give rise to a long‐lived chemiluminescence with emission maxima at 480–500, 570 and 615–650 nm, as well as a paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signal with g‐value at 2.006 and Δ H ∼ 3Gs. Chemiluminescence intensity and EPR signals follow multistep kinetics. An increase of the ratio of OD at 260/400 nm and 400/600 nm and a decrease of amplitude of an EPR signal after prolonged photo‐irradiation were observed. Long irradiation also causes a decrease of fluorescence intensity bands with maxima at 535 nm and 495 nm (Λ ex 480 and 400 nm, respectively), and an increase of the short wavelength band with a maximum at 450 nm (Λ ex 260 nm). The data indicate that a complex chain of reactions initiated by reactive species leads to the degradation of the aromatic core of the polymers. Oxygen efficiently enhances the chemiluminescence intensity and the rate of photodegradation. The mechanism of photodegradative oxidation and chemiluminescence probably involves an energy transfer process and singlet oxygen formation. The possibility of its occurrence in nature and its significance are discussed.

cited_works.title: Rejection of the biophoton hypothesis on the origin of photoreceptor dark noise
cited_works.abstract: Rod photoreceptors of the vertebrate retina produce, in darkness, spontaneous discrete current waves virtually identical to responses to single photons. The waves comprise an irreducible source of noise (discrete dark noise) that may limit the threshold sensitivity of vision. The waves obviously originate from acts of random activation of single rhodopsin molecules. Until recently, it was generally accepted that the activation occurs due to the rhodopsin thermal motion. Yet, a few years ago it was proposed that rhodopsin molecules are activated not by heat but rather by real photons generated within the retina by chemiluminescence. Using a high-sensitive photomultiplier, we measured intensities of biophoton emission from isolated retinas and eyecups of frogs (Rana ridibunda) and fish (sterlet, Acipenser ruthenus). Retinal samples were placed in a perfusion chamber and emitted photons collected by a high-aperture quartz lens. The collected light was sent to the photomultiplier cathode through a rotating chopper so that a long-lasting synchronous accumulation of the light signal was possible. The absolute intensity of bio-emission was estimated by the response of the measuring system to a calibrated light source. The intensity of the source, in turn, was quantified by measuring rhodopsin bleaching with single-rod microspectrophotometry. We also measured the frequency of discrete dark waves in rods of the two species with suction pipette recordings. cited_works.title: Stochastic light concentration from 3D to 2D reveals ultraweak chemi- and bioluminescence
cited_works.abstract: For countless applications in science and technology, light must be concentrated, and concentration is classically achieved with reflective and refractive elements. However, there is so far no efficient way, with a 2D detector, to detect photons produced inside an extended volume with a broad or isotropic angular distribution. Here, with theory and experiment, we propose to stochastically transform and concentrate a volume into a smaller surface, using a high-albedo Ulbricht cavity and a small exit orifice through cavity walls. A 3D gas of photons produced inside the cavity is transformed with a 50% number efficiency into a 2D Lambertian emitting orifice with maximal radiance and a much smaller size. With high-albedo quartz-powder cavity walls ([Formula: see text]), the orifice area is [Formula: see text] times smaller than the walls' area. When coupled to a detectivity-optimized photon-counter ([Formula: see text]) the detection limit is [Formula: see text]. Thanks to this unprecedented sensitivity, we could detect the luminescence produced by the non-catalytic disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide in pure water, which has not been observed so far. We could also detect the ultraweak bioluminescence produced by yeast cells at the onset of their growth. Our work opens new perspectives for studying ultraweak luminescence, and the concept of stochastic 3D/2D conjugation should help design novel light detection methods for large samples or diluted emitters.

cited_works.title: Biological autoluminescence as a noninvasive monitoring tool for chemical and physical modulation of oxidation in yeast cell culture
cited_works.abstract: Normal or excessive oxidative metabolism in organisms is essential in physiological and pathophysiological processes, respectively. Therefore, monitoring of biological oxidative processes induced by the chemical or physical stimuli is nowadays of extreme importance due to the environment overloaded with various physicochemical factors. Current techniques typically require the addition of chemical labels or light illumination, which perturb the samples to be analyzed. Moreover, the current techniques are very demanding in terms of sample preparation and equipment. To alleviate these limitations, we propose a label-free monitoring tool of oxidation based on biological autoluminescence (BAL). We demonstrate this tool on Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell culture. We showed that BAL can be used to monitor chemical perturbation of yeast due to Fenton reagents initiated oxidation-the BAL intensity changes with hydrogen peroxide concentration in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, we also showed that BAL reflects the effects of low-frequency magnetic field on the yeast cell culture, where we observed a disturbance of the BAL kinetics in the exposed vs. control case. Our results contribute to the development of novel techniques for label-free, real-time, noninvasive monitoring of oxidative processes and approaches for their modulation.

cited_works.title: The dark art of light measurement: accurate radiometry for low-level light therapy
cited_works.abstract: Lasers and light-emitting diodes are used for a range of biomedical applications with many studies reporting their beneficial effects. However, three main concerns exist regarding much of the low-level light therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation literature; (1) incomplete, inaccurate and unverified irradiation parameters, (2) miscalculation of 'dose,' and (3) the misuse of appropriate light property terminology. The aim of this systematic review was to assess where, and to what extent, these inadequacies exist and to provide an overview of 'best practice' in light measurement methods and importance of correct light measurement. A review of recent relevant literature was performed in PubMed using the terms LLLT and photobiomodulation (March 2014-March 2015) to investigate the contemporary information available in LLLT and photobiomodulation literature in terms of reporting light properties and irradiation parameters. A total of 74 articles formed the basis of this systematic review. Although most articles reported beneficial effects following LLLT, the majority contained no information in terms of how light was measured (73%) and relied on manufacturer-stated values. For all papers reviewed, missing information for specific light parameters included wavelength (3%), light source type (8%), power (41%), pulse frequency (52%), beam area (40%), irradiance (43%), exposure time (16%), radiant energy (74%) and fluence (16%). cited_works.title: Biophotonic evaluation of water treated by biodynamization: comparison of ultra-low emission levels in the 300–400 nm, 400–500 nm and 500–600 nm bands on different types of water
cited_works.abstract: This study examines the spontaneous ultraweak photon (UWP) emission observed in water treated by the Biodynamizer dynamization system (SA Dynamized Technologies) in the 300–400 nm, 400–500 nm, and 500–600 nm spectra. This study follows up on biophotonic results observed in the 435–500 nm band and more broadly in the 380–630 nm spectrum, which were obtained and published in a scientific journal in November 2025. The objective of this new study was to evaluate more precisely new biophotonic emission spectra, to study the links between wavelength and human physiology and to look at the correlations between our study and the results of analyses and expert assessments carried out according to the electrophotonic analysis method (EPA: Electrophotonic Analysis) whose reproducibility of the method has allowed to be validated from a scientific point of view after peer review on the occasion of the publication by the journal Substantia of the article “ ElectroPhotonic Analysis (EPA) of tap water droplets versus hydroalcoholic solutions ”. The measurements were performed using a Berthold Lumat LB 9508 luminometer, equipped with borosilicate glass tubes and bandpass optical filters (300–400 nm, 400–500 nm, and 500–600 nm). All experiments were conducted under controlled conditions at the Enerlab laboratory (Nice, France) on December 1 and 2, 2025. Photon emission intensities are expressed in relative light units (RLU). cited_works.title: Comparative analysis of ultra-weak photon emission in the 380–630 nm band in germinated seeds watered with different waters
cited_works.abstract: This study evaluates the influence of the physico-energetic quality of water on germination processes and ultra-low biophotonic emission (UPE) of Alfalfa seeds (Medicago sativa L.). The water samples tested included:(1) mains water, (2) reverse osmosis water, (3) commercial mineral water, and (4) water filtered and revitalized by the OJADE Biophotons 369 system, designed to restructure water via a process combining filtration, vortexing and exposure to coherent photonic fields. The seeds were grown in standard germinators and watered daily with different waters throughout the germination phase. Ultra-weak photon emissions were measured using a Berthold LUMAT LB 9508 luminometer, in the spectral range 380–630 nm. The results show that seeds watered with water from the OJADE Biophotons 369 system exhibit significantly higher biophotonic emission than those watered with other types of water. This increase is correlated with enhanced metabolic and bioenergetic activity, suggesting improved efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and redox signaling processes. Vitalized water thus appears to act as a coherent carrier of photonic energy, promoting intracellular and intercellular light communication in plant tissues. These observations support the hypothesis that the photodynamic structuring of water can influence biological processes through coherent interactions between the electromagnetic fields of water and those of living systems. Further research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms and the reproducibility of these effects in other plant models.

cited_works.title: Measuring the Human Ultra-Weak Photon Emission Distribution Using an Electron-Multiplying, Charge-Coupled Device as a Sensor
cited_works.abstract: Ultra-weak photon emission (UPE) is the spontaneous emission from living systems mainly attributed to oxidation reactions, in which reactive oxygen species (ROS) may play a major role. Given the capability of the next-generation electron-multiplying CCD (EMCCD) sensors and the easy use of liquid crystal tunable filters (LCTF), the aim of this work was to explore the potential of a simple UPE spectrometer to measure the UPE from a human hand. Thus, an easy setup was configured based on a dark box for inserting the subject’s hand prior to LCTF as a monochromator and an EMCCD sensor working in the full vertical binning mode (FVB) as a spectra detector. Under controlled conditions, both dark signals and left hand UPE were acquired by registering the UPE intensity at different selected wavelengths (400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 650, and 700 nm) during a period of 10 min each. Then, spurious signals were filtered out by ignoring the pixels whose values were clearly outside of the Gaussian distribution, and the dark signal was subtracted from the subject hand signal. The stepped spectrum with a peak of approximately 880 photons at 500 nm had a shape that agreed somewhat with previous reports, and agrees with previous UPE research that reported UPE from 420 to 570 nm, or 260 to 800 nm, with a range from 1 to 1000 photons s−1 cm−2. Obtaining the spectral distribution instead of the total intensity of the UPE represents a step forward in this field, as it may provide extra information about a subject’s personal states and relationship with ROS. cited_works.title: Imaging Ultraweak Photon Emission from Living and Dead Mice and from Plants under Stress
cited_works.abstract: The phenomenon of biological ultraweak photon emission (UPE), that is, extremely low-intensity emission (10 − 10 3 photons/cm 2 /sec) in the spectral range of 200 − 1000 nm, has been observed in all living systems that have been examined. Here we report experiments that exemplify the ability of novel imaging systems to detect variations in UPE for a set of physiologically important scenarios. We use EMCCD and CCD cameras to capture single visible-wavelength photons with low noise and quantum efficiencies higher than 90%. Our investigation reveals significant contrast between the UPE from live vs. dead mice. In plants we observed that an increase in temperature and injuries both caused an increase in UPE intensity. Moreover, chemical treatments modified the UPE emission characteristics of plants, particularly the application of an anesthetic (benzocaine) to injury, which showed the highest emission among the compounds tested. As a result, UPE imaging provides the possibility of non-invasive label-free imaging of vitality in animals and the responses of plants to stress.

statement: The wavelength-band ratios that the human-UPE literature uses to discriminate clinical groups are artefacts of the detector's spectral response: recomputing the published 495 nm / 550 nm cut-off-filter ratio after correcting for the measured (not nominal) filter transmission and the detector's per-band quantum efficiency changes the ratio by more than the reported between-group difference, and the healthy-versus-patient discrimination does not survive the correction.

scope.population: Adult humans, fingertip and dorsal-hand surface UPE, healthy controls versus a defined clinical group (common cold, or type-2 diabetes)
scope.condition: Cut-off-filter or bandpass photon counting over 400-700 nm with per-band QE and per-filter transmission measured on the actual instrument
scope.comparator: The same raw photocount data analysed without spectral-response correction, i.e. the published analysis
scope.outcome: Corrected band ratio and its between-group difference with 95% CI, versus the uncorrected band ratio and its between-group difference

null_hypothesis: The spectral-response correction shifts the band ratios by less than the between-group difference and the group discrimination survives with its effect size substantially intact, in which case the spectral-information claim is robust to the metrology gap and H11 is strengthened rather than undermined.
estimand: Delta_corrected - Delta_uncorrected, where Delta is the standardised between-group difference in the band ratio; and the correction factor C = eta_bar(band A)/eta_bar(band B) applied to each ratio.
proposed_experiment: Re-run the two-hand cut-off-filter protocol on matched healthy and clinical cohorts (n >= 20 per group), but measure on the actual instrument: (i) eta(lambda) at 10 nm resolution against an SPDC- or calibrated-source-referenced standard, (ii) each filter's transmission spectrum on the same optical path, (iii) the dark spectrum. Compute band ratios twice from identical raw counts - once as published, once fully corrected - and compare the two between-group effect sizes with a paired bootstrap on the same subjects. Independently repeat the spectral measurement with an EMCCD behind a liquid-crystal tunable filter to obtain a correction-independent spectrum on the same hands in the same session.

rationale.step: The discriminating study itself publishes its instrument's per-band quantum efficiencies: 27% (290-395 nm), 23% (395-455 nm), 15% (455-495 nm), 6% (495-550 nm), 3% (550 nm and above), and reports its discrimination as a photon-emission ratio between the 550 nm and 495 nm filters.

Computation. An uncorrected count ratio between two bands is the true photon-number ratio multiplied by eta_bar(A)/eta_bar(B). For the 455-495 nm versus 495-550 nm pair that factor is 15/6 = 2.5; for the 395-455 nm versus >550 nm pair it is 23/3 = 7.7. The published between-group differences in such ratios are far smaller than 2.5x, so any inter-instrument difference in QE roll-off - or any error in the assumed effective band edges - is large enough to create or destroy the reported discrimination.

Correcting only with manufacturer-stated transmission values is current practice and is insufficient: a plant-UPE study explicitly normalised measured photon counts by each filter's manufacturer-provided average transmission, and the same study reports that PMT photocathode radiant-sensitivity limits prevented accurate analysis over 700-720 nm.

Independent confirmation that instrument spectral response, not source spectrum, dominates the reported band content: a 2026 re-analysis of head UPE shows photons below 600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull while longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the PMTs used, so the recovered 'spectrum' is a product of two steep and opposite roll-offs.

The measurement is buildable now with better spectral control than cut-off filters: an EMCCD behind a liquid-crystal tunable filter has already been used to record human-hand UPE at 400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 650 and 700 nm, and the authors themselves note that non-uniform spectral transmittance of the spectrograph is the limiting factor to be fixed.
The clinical stakes are concrete because band-ratio and spectral features feed published diagnostic claims for type-2 diabetes and for traditional-medicine subtyping.

cited_works.title: Spectral discrimination between healthy people and cold patients using spontaneous photon emission
cited_works.abstract: In this paper, ultra-weak photon emission (UPE) was used to distinguish cold patients from healthy subjects. The UPE intensity of fingertips of two hands from healthy subjects and cold patients was measured using a two-hand UPE detecting system and a group of cut-off filters. We found a significant difference in the maximum spectral peak and photon emission ratio between the filter of 550nm and 495nm, which can be used in distinguish cold patients from healthy people. Methods and results in this work could be useful for developing a new optical diagnostic tool for early disease diagnosis in the future.

cited_works.title: Leaf wound induced ultraweak photon emission is suppressed under anoxic stress: Observations of Spathiphyllum under aerobic and anaerobic conditions using novel in vivo methodology
cited_works.abstract: Plants have evolved a variety of means to energetically sense and respond to abiotic and biotic environmental stress. Two typical photochemical signaling responses involve the emission of volatile organic compounds and light. The emission of certain leaf wound volatiles and light are mutually dependent upon oxygen which is subsequently required for the wound-induced lipoxygenase reactions that trigger the formation of fatty acids and hydroperoxides; ultimately leading to photon emission by chlorophyll molecules. A low noise photomultiplier with sensitivity in the visible spectrum (300-720 nm) is used to continuously measure long duration ultraweak photon emission of dark-adapting whole Spathiphyllum leaves (in vivo). Leaves were mechanically wounded after two hours of dark adaptation in aerobic and anaerobic conditions. It was found that (1) nitrogen incubation did not affect the pre-wound basal photocounts; (2) wound induced leaf biophoton emission was significantly suppressed when under anoxic stress; and (3) the aerobic wound induced emission spectra observed was > 650 nm, implicating chlorophyll as the likely emitter. Limitations of the PMT photocathode's radiant sensitivity, however, prevented accurate analysis from 700-720 nm. Further examination of leaf wounding profile photon counts revealed that the pre-wounding basal state (aerobic and anoxic), the anoxic wounding state, and the post-wounding aerobic state statistics all approximate a Poisson distribution. cited_works.title: Revisiting Claims of Extracranial Biophoton Detection from the Human Brain
cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

cited_works.title: The application and trend of ultra-weak photon emission in biology and medicine
cited_works.abstract: Ultra-weak bioluminescence, also known as ultra-weak photon emission (UPE), is one of the functional characteristics of biological organisms, characterized by specialized, low-energy level luminescence. Researchers have extensively studied UPE for decades, and the mechanisms by which UPE is generated and its properties have been extensively investigated. However, there has been a gradual shift in research focus on UPE in recent years toward exploring its application value. To better understand the application and trend of UPE in biology and medicine, we have conducted a review of relevant articles in recent years. Among the several topics covered in this review is UPE research in biology and medicine (including traditional Chinese medicine), primarily focused on UPE as a promising non-invasive tool for diagnosis and oxidative metabolism monitoring as well as a potential tool for traditional Chinese medicine research.

statement: Under properly light-tight conditions with absolute-unit reporting, the excess surface photon flux measured from a human head is reproduced within a factor of two by a thermally and optically matched inanimate phantom, establishing that reported extracranial 'brain UPE' magnitudes are set by the measurement environment rather than by the brain.

scope.population: Healthy adult volunteers (n >= 15), occipital and temporal scalp; plus a head phantom matched for surface reflectance, emissivity and surface temperature 35-37 C, plus an empty light-tight chamber
scope.condition: Photon counting in a fully dark-adapted, verified light-tight enclosure, 400-700 nm on a PMT arm and 600-1000 nm on a silicon SPAD/EMCCD arm, with dark count rate, QE and collection geometry declared and the result reported in photons s-1 cm-2
scope.comparator: Matched phantom in the identical chamber and session; empty-chamber blank; and the same protocol run with a deliberately imperfect seal to quantify the contamination channel
scope.outcome: Absolute surface photon flux density (photons s-1 cm-2, per band) for head, phantom and blank, with 95% CI

null_hypothesis: Head excess flux exceeds phantom excess flux by more than a factor of two, in a band where scalp and skull transmit and the detector responds, and this persists across sessions and seal conditions - i.e. a genuine biological head signal survives the phantom control and the contamination explanation fails.
estimand: Ratio Phi_head / Phi_phantom in absolute photons s-1 cm-2 per spectral band, with 95% CI; plus the fraction of previously published head-UPE magnitudes reproduced by the phantom arm.
proposed_experiment: In one light-tight, verified-sealed chamber, alternate within a single session between (i) a dark-adapted volunteer's scalp, (ii) a temperature-controlled head phantom at 36 C with matched surface reflectance, and (iii) an empty chamber, randomising order across >=15 volunteers. Run two detector arms simultaneously on the same surface patch: a cooled PMT (400-700 nm) and a silicon SPAD or EMCCD (600-1000 nm). Report every result as photons s-1 cm-2 with declared eta(lambda), D, dead time and collection solid angle. Add a deliberate calibrated leak condition to measure the contamination transfer function. Decision rule: contamination explanation is supported if Phi_head / Phi_phantom <= 2 in every band; refuted if the ratio exceeds 2 in a transmitting, detector-responsive band and replicates across sessions.

rationale.step: A 2026 analysis reports that under properly dark conditions the UPE from the head is much weaker than values published in the brain-UPE literature, that the large reported signals can be explained by background light contamination, and that even a genuine background-free head signal would be dominated by scalp rather than brain as long as PMTs are used.

That analysis performs exactly the absolute conversion the rest of the field omits - quantum efficiency 0.23 applied and an average dark count rate of 22 counts/s subtracted before computing flux - which is what makes its refutation quantitative rather than rhetorical.

The claims at issue are live and are being built upon: head/brain UPE is proposed as a non-electrical modality for investigating brain function, as the read-out for a skull-implant photonic brain-computer interface, and as an emotional-state and imagined-light correlate in human head measurements.

Computation of the phantom's required match. A blackbody at 37 C contributes negligibly in the visible: the characterisation of an EM-CCD as a binary photon counter finds non-negligible sensitivity to blackbody radiation only above T = 50 C. Therefore a phantom matched to 35-37 C isolates the non-thermal contamination channel (stray light leakage, chamber-material afterglow, detector-window luminescence) rather than confounding it with thermal emission, and any residual difference between head and phantom in the 400-700 nm band cannot be attributed to temperature.

Computation of the spectral trap. The head measurement is squeezed between two roll-offs: tissue attenuation removes the short-wavelength half of the band while PMT cathode sensitivity removes the long-wavelength half. A detector arm extending to 1000 nm (silicon SPAD or back-illuminated EMCCD with >90% QE across the visible) is therefore required to test whether any surviving head signal sits in the window where tissue transmits but a PMT does not respond - a band no published head-UPE study has covered.

Detectors with the needed long-wavelength reach and absolute characterisability are demonstrated in this corpus on whole-animal and whole-plant samples: EMCCD/CCD systems with QE >90-95% across the visible and dark current on the order of 1e-4 have already imaged UPE contrast between live and dead mice.

cited_works.title: Revisiting Claims of Extracranial Biophoton Detection from the Human Brain
cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

Therefore, we propose a novel skull implant BCI that uses UPE. cited_works.title: Increment of spontaneous human biophoton emission caused by anger emotional states. Proof of concept
cited_works.abstract: Humans spontaneously emit visible radiation from their skin, which is known as biophoton or ultra-weak photon emission (UPE). Up to date, UPE intensity changes according to different external and internal factors have been reported. However, the influence in the human UPE of negative emotional states has never been studied despite their clinic and forensic interest. In this work, an ad hoc system based on a high-sensitive CCD detector was developed to detect and image UPE from human’s upper body. Then, the UPE emitted by the upper part of the body of nine volunteers was imaged in two different personal states: (i) when subjects were feeling relaxed; and (ii) when they were emotionally stimulated to feel anger. For all the volunteers, the relative measurement of UPE intensity was higher when feeling anger than when feeling relaxed. Due to the relevance of this disruptive idea and the horizon this knowledge can provide, this proof of concept must be followed by further experiments. An increase in the number of subjects will be accomplished in order to enhance these preliminary results and propose UPE as a new physiological parameter of negative emotional states.

statement: A UPE-based diagnostic classifier trained at one site loses more than half its AUC when applied to a second site using a different detector class, and re-expressing the same features in absolute, spectrally-corrected units (photons s-1 cm-2 per band) recovers at least half of the lost AUC - showing that the field's diagnostic non-transfer is dominated by the missing calibration chain rather than by the biology.

scope.population: Adults with early-stage type-2 diabetes and matched healthy controls (n >= 60 per site), fingertip and dorsal-hand surface UPE
scope.condition: Two independent sites, deliberately different detector classes (cooled PMT photon counter at site A, EMCCD at site B), identical sampling protocol, dark adaptation and anatomical landmarks
scope.comparator: Same classifier evaluated (i) within-site out-of-sample, (ii) cross-site on raw instrument-native counts, (iii) cross-site on absolute spectrally-corrected features
scope.outcome: Out-of-sample AUC in each of the three settings, with 95% CI by site-level bootstrap

null_hypothesis: Absolute-unit re-expression recovers less than half the lost cross-site AUC (recovery fraction < 0.5), meaning the non-transfer is driven by biological, protocol or population differences and calibration is not the binding constraint - which would remove the metrology explanation for the field's diagnostic irreproducibility.
estimand: Recovery fraction R = (AUC_cross_absolute - AUC_cross_raw) / (AUC_within - AUC_cross_raw), with 95% CI.
proposed_experiment: Prospective two-site study with deliberately mismatched detector classes. Site A (cooled PMT, 300-650 nm) and Site B (EMCCD, 400-900 nm) each recruit >=60 early-stage T2D and >=60 matched controls under one shared clinical and dark-adaptation protocol. Both sites measure eta(lambda), dark rate, dead time, filter transmission and collection geometry in-house against a common transfer standard, and archive raw counts. Train a locked classifier at Site A; evaluate within-site out-of-sample, then cross-site twice - once on raw counts, once after converting both sites' archived raw counts to photons s-1 cm-2 per band. Report R with a site-level bootstrap CI. Pre-register R >= 0.5 as support.

rationale.step: Given by the seed brief: the field lists the absence of standardized protocols for clinical measurement among its key experimental constraints, and states that UPE remains a technical curiosity rather than a reliable biomarker without standardization.

Single-site UPE diagnostic claims for type-2 diabetes exist and are the natural training set: UPE has been reported to distinguish healthy subjects from type-2 diabetes patients, proposed as a non-invasive tool for detecting early-stage type-2 diabetes, and combined with plasma metabolomics for subtyping pre-diabetes.

The field has never had an evaluation instrument for this kind of claim: a systematic review of 56 included human-UPE studies (1 RCT, 27 CCT, 28 observational) concluded that a tool for systematically evaluating this bio-evaluation methodology is not currently available and would be worth developing - i.e. no site-transfer criterion exists.

The two detector classes named differ in exactly the parameters that would break raw-count transfer: PMT arms in this literature run at QE ~0.23 with tens of dark counts per second, while EMCCD arms run at QE >0.90 with dark current four orders of magnitude lower, and each has a different spectral weighting.

Computation of the expected AUC damage. A classifier boundary on raw counts is a threshold on C = Phi * A_eff * g * eta_bar * T. Moving to a detector with a different eta_bar rescales C multiplicatively and, because eta_bar is wavelength-dependent, differentially across features - so a linear boundary in raw-count feature space is both translated and sheared. A 2-4x multiplicative shift with a differential band weighting of up to 2.5x (from published per-band QE of 15% versus 6%) is more than enough to push a boundary tuned to a within-site separation of well under one decade to chance. Absolute-unit re-expression removes the multiplicative term exactly and the shear to the accuracy of the measured eta(lambda), which is why R is the informative quantity.

Absolute-unit reporting is achievable at both sites with existing hardware and existing precedent: absolute bio-emission intensity has been obtained by referencing a photon-counting system to a calibrated light source, and national metrology institutes provide traceable or absolute calibration of single-photon detectors and sources.

cited_works.title: Ultraweak Photon Emission as a Non-Invasive Health Assessment: A Systematic Review
cited_works.abstract: We conducted a systematic review (SR) of the peer reviewed scientific literature on ultraweak photon emissions (UPE) from humans. The question was: Can ultraweak photon emissions from humans be used as a non-invasive health assessment? A systematic search was conducted across eight relevant databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, BIOSIS, CINAHL, PSYCHINFO, All of Cochrane EBM databases, GIDEON, DoD Biomedical Research, and clinicaltrials.gov from database inception to October 2011. Of the 1315 studies captured by the search strategy, 56 met the inclusion criteria, out of which 1 was a RCT, 27 were CCT, and 28 were observational and descriptive studies. There were no systematic reviews/meta-analyses that fit the inclusion criteria. In this report, the authors provide an assessment of the quality of the RCT included; describe the characteristics of all the included studies, the outcomes assessed, and the effectiveness of photon emission as a potential health assessment tool. This report demonstrates that the peer reviewed literature on UPE and human UPE measurement in particular is surprisingly large. Most of the human UPE literature is of good to high quality based on our systematic evaluation. However, an evaluation tool for systematically evaluating this type of "bio-evaluation" methodology is not currently available and would be worth developing. cited_works.abstract: In this paper, ultra-weak photon emission (UPE) was used to distinguish cold patients from healthy subjects. The UPE intensity of fingertips of two hands from healthy subjects and cold patients was measured using a two-hand UPE detecting system and a group of cut-off filters. We found a significant difference in the maximum spectral peak and photon emission ratio between the filter of 550nm and 495nm, which can be used in distinguish cold patients from healthy people. Methods and results in this work could be useful for developing a new optical diagnostic tool for early disease diagnosis in the future.

cited_works.abstract: Rod photoreceptors of the vertebrate retina produce, in darkness, spontaneous discrete current waves virtually identical to responses to single photons. The waves comprise an irreducible source of noise (discrete dark noise) that may limit the threshold sensitivity of vision. The waves obviously originate from acts of random activation of single rhodopsin molecules. Until recently, it was generally accepted that the activation occurs due to the rhodopsin thermal motion. Yet, a few years ago it was proposed that rhodopsin molecules are activated not by heat but rather by real photons generated within the retina by chemiluminescence. Using a high-sensitive photomultiplier, we measured intensities of biophoton emission from isolated retinas and eyecups of frogs (Rana ridibunda) and fish (sterlet, Acipenser ruthenus). Retinal samples were placed in a perfusion chamber and emitted photons collected by a high-aperture quartz lens. The collected light was sent to the photomultiplier cathode through a rotating chopper so that a long-lasting synchronous accumulation of the light signal was possible. The absolute intensity of bio-emission was estimated by the response of the measuring system to a calibrated light source. The intensity of the source, in turn, was quantified by measuring rhodopsin bleaching with single-rod microspectrophotometry. We also measured the frequency of discrete dark waves in rods of the two species with suction pipette recordings. cited_works.title: Photon-number correlation for quantum enhanced imaging and sensing
cited_works.abstract: In this review we present the potentialities and the achievements of the use of non-classical photon-number correlations in twin-beam states for many applications, ranging from imaging to metrology. Photon-number correlations in the quantum regime are easily produced and are rather robust against unavoidable experimental losses, and noise in some cases, if compared to the entanglement, where losing one photon can completely compromise the state and its exploitable advantages. Here, we will focus on quantum enhanced protocols in which only phase-insensitive intensity measurements (photon-number counting) are performed, which allow probing the transmission/absorption properties of a system, leading, for example, to innovative target detection schemes in a strong background. In this framework, one of the advantages is that the sources experimentally available emit a wide number of pair-wise correlated modes, which can be intercepted and exploited separately, for example by many pixels of a camera, providing a parallelism, essential in several applications, such as wide-field sub-shot-noise imaging and quantum enhanced ghost imaging. Finally, non-classical correlation enables new possibilities in quantum radiometry, e.g. the possibility of absolute calibration of a spatial resolving detector from the on-off single-photon regime to the linear regime in the same setup.

statement: Spontaneous UPE has a conserved absolute photon yield per unit oxidative turnover: in a chemically defined preparation the ratio of emitted photons (4 pi, 350-700 nm) to moles of oxidant consumed is reproducible within a factor of three across laboratories and detector classes, and this yield, multiplied by an independently measured cellular ROS flux, accounts for the observed spontaneous emission of the same culture within a factor of ten.

scope.population: Saccharomyces cerevisiae culture at defined density in defined medium, with a Fe(II)/H2O2 Fenton oxidative challenge across a dose series; secondary preparation: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii with exogenous linoleic acid driving lipid peroxidation
scope.condition: Absolute photon counting, 350-700 nm, with declared eta(lambda), dark rate and collection solid angle, run in parallel with an independent chemical assay of oxidant consumption or peroxidation product accumulation on aliquots of the same culture
scope.comparator: Cell-free medium with the identical Fenton challenge (the non-biological chemiexcitation baseline), and unchallenged culture
scope.outcome: Photon yield Phi_UPE = photons s-1 (4 pi, 350-700 nm) per mol s-1 of oxidant consumed, with 95% CI, per laboratory and detector class

null_hypothesis: Phi_UPE varies by more than one order of magnitude between laboratories, or between chemically identical preparations measured on different detector classes, or the yield fails to predict spontaneous emission of the same culture within a factor of ten - in which case absolute units do not buy mechanistic comparability and the oxidative-origin account cannot be closed as a photon budget.
estimand: Phi_UPE (dimensionless photons per oxidant molecule) with 95% CI; and the ratio of predicted to observed spontaneous emission rate for the same culture.
proposed_experiment: In each of >=3 laboratories with different detector classes, run a Fenton dose series on a common S. cerevisiae strain at fixed OD in defined medium, measuring absolute photon emission (350-700 nm, converted to photons s-1 into 4 pi using measured eta(lambda), collection solid angle and transmission) while assaying H2O2 consumption on parallel aliquots by a standard peroxide assay, plus the cell-free medium control at each dose. Compute the regression slope in absolute units - that slope is Phi_UPE. Independently, measure the same culture's spontaneous emission and its baseline ROS flux, and test whether Phi_UPE * J predicts the observed spontaneous rate within 10x. Repeat the numerator/denominator pairing in Chlamydomonas with linoleic acid and TBARS. Refutation: between-laboratory spread of Phi_UPE > 1 decade, or prediction error > 10x.

rationale.step: The dose-response arm already exists: biological autoluminescence intensity in a S. cerevisiae culture changes with hydrogen peroxide concentration in a dose-dependent manner under Fenton-reagent-initiated oxidation, and the same platform has been developed as a label-free, perturbance-free oxidation monitor.

The chemistry-only baseline for the same denominator is documented: the non-catalytic disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide in pure water produces luminescence detectable with a detectivity-optimised photon counter coupled to a high-albedo Ulbricht cavity, giving a cell-free control that fixes how much of the yield is chemiexcitation rather than biology.

A paired photon/chemistry measurement of the required kind has already been performed in a second organism: linoleic-acid-induced UPE from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii was shown to correlate with lipid peroxidation product accumulation measured by thiobarbituric acid assay, with hydroxyl-radical scavenging, lipoxygenase inhibition and oxygen removal each suppressing emission - so the numerator and denominator can be measured on the same culture.

The chemiexcitation physics that sets the yield is characterised in the corpus: cyclic-peroxide (1,2-dioxetane and 1,2-dioxetanone) fragmentation preferentially populates triplet or singlet excited product states with quantum yields well below unity, and luminol serves as the calibration standard for the detecting PMT - meaning the yield is a defined chemical quantity, not a free parameter.

Computation of why the yield, not the intensity, is the comparable quantity. Measured count rate C depends on Phi_UPE, the oxidative flux J, and the instrument factor (A_eff * g * eta_bar * T). Two laboratories reporting C differ by both biology (J) and instrument. Dividing the absolute emission rate by an independently assayed J cancels the biological driver and leaves Phi_UPE, which is a property of the chemistry alone; therefore any residual between-laboratory spread in Phi_UPE beyond the stated assay uncertainty is, by construction, instrumental. A factor-of-three tolerance is the right threshold because it is smaller than the ~1.4-decade spread that unreported g, eta_bar and T can generate but larger than the assay's own reproducibility.

The claim is currently untestable in the literature because emission is not reported in absolute units: reported spontaneous UPE spans 1-1000 and 10-10^3 photons s-1 cm-2 across sources with no shared conversion, and some current measurement reports give only relative light units.

cited_works.title: Biological autoluminescence as a noninvasive monitoring tool for chemical and physical modulation of oxidation in yeast cell culture
cited_works.abstract: Normal or excessive oxidative metabolism in organisms is essential in physiological and pathophysiological processes, respectively. Therefore, monitoring of biological oxidative processes induced by the chemical or physical stimuli is nowadays of extreme importance due to the environment overloaded with various physicochemical factors. Current techniques typically require the addition of chemical labels or light illumination, which perturb the samples to be analyzed. Moreover, the current techniques are very demanding in terms of sample preparation and equipment. To alleviate these limitations, we propose a label-free monitoring tool of oxidation based on biological autoluminescence (BAL). We demonstrate this tool on Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell culture. We showed that BAL can be used to monitor chemical perturbation of yeast due to Fenton reagents initiated oxidation-the BAL intensity changes with hydrogen peroxide concentration in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, we also showed that BAL reflects the effects of low-frequency magnetic field on the yeast cell culture, where we observed a disturbance of the BAL kinetics in the exposed vs. control case. Our results contribute to the development of novel techniques for label-free, real-time, noninvasive monitoring of oxidative processes and approaches for their modulation.

cited_works.abstract: For countless applications in science and technology, light must be concentrated, and concentration is classically achieved with reflective and refractive elements. However, there is so far no efficient way, with a 2D detector, to detect photons produced inside an extended volume with a broad or isotropic angular distribution. Here, with theory and experiment, we propose to stochastically transform and concentrate a volume into a smaller surface, using a high-albedo Ulbricht cavity and a small exit orifice through cavity walls. A 3D gas of photons produced inside the cavity is transformed with a 50% number efficiency into a 2D Lambertian emitting orifice with maximal radiance and a much smaller size. With high-albedo quartz-powder cavity walls ([Formula: see text]), the orifice area is [Formula: see text] times smaller than the walls' area. When coupled to a detectivity-optimized photon-counter ([Formula: see text]) the detection limit is [Formula: see text]. Thanks to this unprecedented sensitivity, we could detect the luminescence produced by the non-catalytic disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide in pure water, which has not been observed so far. We could also detect the ultraweak bioluminescence produced by yeast cells at the onset of their growth. Our work opens new perspectives for studying ultraweak luminescence, and the concept of stochastic 3D/2D conjugation should help design novel light detection methods for large samples or diluted emitters.

cited_works.title: Chemi- and Bioluminescence of Cyclic Peroxides
cited_works.abstract: Bioluminescence is a phenomenon that has fascinated mankind for centuries. Today the phenomenon and its sibling, chemiluminescence, have impacted society with a number of useful applications in fields like analytical chemistry and medicine, just to mention two. In this review, a molecular-orbital perspective is adopted to explain the chemistry behind chemiexcitation in both chemi- and bioluminescence. First, the uncatalyzed thermal dissociation of 1,2-dioxetane is presented and analyzed to explain, for example, the preference for triplet excited product states and increased yield with larger nonreactive substituents. The catalyzed fragmentation reaction and related details are then exemplified with substituted 1,2-dioxetanone species. In particular, the preference for singlet excited product states in that case is explained. The review also examines the diversity of specific solutions both in Nature and in artificial systems and the difficulties in identifying the emitting species and unraveling the color modulation process. The related subject of excited-state chemistry without light absorption is finally discussed. The content of this review should be an inspiration to human design of new molecular systems expressing unique light-emitting properties. An appendix describing the state-of-the-art experimental and theoretical methods used to study the phenomena serves as a complement.

Thus, an easy setup was configured based on a dark box for inserting the subject’s hand prior to LCTF as a monochromator and an EMCCD sensor working in the full vertical binning mode (FVB) as a spectra detector. Under controlled conditions, both dark signals and left hand UPE were acquired by registering the UPE intensity at different selected wavelengths (400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 650, and 700 nm) during a period of 10 min each. Then, spurious signals were filtered out by ignoring the pixels whose values were clearly outside of the Gaussian distribution, and the dark signal was subtracted from the subject hand signal. The stepped spectrum with a peak of approximately 880 photons at 500 nm had a shape that agreed somewhat with previous reports, and agrees with previous UPE research that reported UPE from 420 to 570 nm, or 260 to 800 nm, with a range from 1 to 1000 photons s−1 cm−2. cited_works.title: Imaging Ultraweak Photon Emission from Living and Dead Mice and from Plants under Stress
cited_works.abstract: The phenomenon of biological ultraweak photon emission (UPE), that is, extremely low-intensity emission (10 − 10 3 photons/cm 2 /sec) in the spectral range of 200 − 1000 nm, has been observed in all living systems that have been examined. Here we report experiments that exemplify the ability of novel imaging systems to detect variations in UPE for a set of physiologically important scenarios. We use EMCCD and CCD cameras to capture single visible-wavelength photons with low noise and quantum efficiencies higher than 90%. Our investigation reveals significant contrast between the UPE from live vs. dead mice. In plants we observed that an increase in temperature and injuries both caused an increase in UPE intensity. Moreover, chemical treatments modified the UPE emission characteristics of plants, particularly the application of an anesthetic (benzocaine) to injury, which showed the highest emission among the compounds tested. As a result, UPE imaging provides the possibility of non-invasive label-free imaging of vitality in animals and the responses of plants to stress.

cited_works.title: Phenomenological Interpretations of Some Somatic Temporal and Spatial Patterns of Biophoton Emission in Humans
cited_works.abstract: Biophoton emission remains controversial. The photo-genic origin of biophoton has been attributed to the oxidative stress or free radical production. However, there are considerable gaps in quantitative understanding of biophoton emission. I propose an analytical hypothesis for interpreting a few patterns of steady-state biophoton emission of human, including the dependency on age, the diurnal variation, and the geometric asymmetry associated with serious asymmetrical pathological conditions. The hypothesis is based on an alternative form of energy state, termed vivo-nergy, which is associated with only metabolically active organisms that are also under neuronal control. The hypothesis projects a decrease of the vivo-nergy in human during growth beyond puberty. The hypothesis also proposes a modification of the vivo-nergy by the phases of systematic or homeostatic physiology. The hypothesis further postulates that the deviation of the physiology-modified vivo-nergy from the pre-puberty level is deteriorated by acquired organ-specific pathological conditions. A temporal differential change of vivo-nergy is hypothesized to proportionally modulate oxidative stress that functions as the physical source of biophoton emission. The resulted steady-state diffusion of the photon emitted from a photo-genic source in a human geometry simplified as a homogeneous spherical domain is modeled by photon diffusion principles incorporating an extrapolated zero-boundary condition. cited_works.title: Comparative analysis of ultra-weak photon emission in the 380–630 nm band in germinated seeds watered with different waters
cited_works.abstract: This study evaluates the influence of the physico-energetic quality of water on germination processes and ultra-low biophotonic emission (UPE) of Alfalfa seeds (Medicago sativa L.). The water samples tested included:(1) mains water, (2) reverse osmosis water, (3) commercial mineral water, and (4) water filtered and revitalized by the OJADE Biophotons 369 system, designed to restructure water via a process combining filtration, vortexing and exposure to coherent photonic fields. The seeds were grown in standard germinators and watered daily with different waters throughout the germination phase. Ultra-weak photon emissions were measured using a Berthold LUMAT LB 9508 luminometer, in the spectral range 380–630 nm. The results show that seeds watered with water from the OJADE Biophotons 369 system exhibit significantly higher biophotonic emission than those watered with other types of water. This increase is correlated with enhanced metabolic and bioenergetic activity, suggesting improved efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and redox signaling processes. Vitalized water thus appears to act as a coherent carrier of photonic energy, promoting intracellular and intercellular light communication in plant tissues. These observations support the hypothesis that the photodynamic structuring of water can influence biological processes through coherent interactions between the electromagnetic fields of water and those of living systems. Further research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms and the reproducibility of these effects in other plant models.

statement: For mechanically wounded seven-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana, independently calibrated PMT and EMCCD measurements of the 400–870 nm photon-emission-rate-density integral over the first 30 minutes after incision will be equivalent within ±15%.

scope.population: Seven-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana plants, with at least 30 plants per detector comparison
scope.condition: Two-hour dark adaptation followed by a standardized sharp leaf incision and simultaneous 30-minute acquisition
scope.comparator: A red-sensitive photon-counting PMT versus a back-illuminated EMCCD viewing the same leaf through a calibrated beam splitter
scope.outcome: Background-subtracted 400–870 nm photon emission per second per square centimetre, integrated over 30 minutes

null_hypothesis: The 90% confidence interval for the PMT-to-EMCCD mean emission-density ratio is not wholly contained within 0.85–1.15.
estimand: Ratio of geometric-mean calibrated 30-minute emission-density integrals from the PMT and EMCCD.
proposed_experiment: Calibrate both detector paths with the same wavelength-scanned low-flux transfer source, measure beam-splitter ratio and collection geometry, then acquire injured leaves and shuttered dark frames simultaneously. Convert both count streams to photon s^-1 cm^-2 and perform a preregistered paired equivalence test with bounds 0.85–1.15.

rationale.step: The seed brief identifies the absence of absolute photon units and direct instrument comparability as the metrology hole.
Standardized incision of seven-week-old Arabidopsis produces measurable UPE extending through 400–870 nm, with a dominant 700–750 nm contribution.

This study refines the spectral analysis of UPE in 7-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana plants subjected to mechanical injury, directly addressing well-documented detection challenges in the longer-wavelength regions and enhancing the utility of UPE as a biomarker for oxidative damage. Previous investigations utilized cut-on absorption filters and CCD imaging, which suffered from imprecise spectral resolution due to poor filter characteristics and reliance on subtraction methods for band emission computation. statement: For wounded Arabidopsis thaliana leaves, replacing wavelength-resolved response correction with a single quantum-efficiency value specified at 500 nm will bias the inferred 400–870 nm photon-emission-rate density by at least 25%.

scope.condition: First 30 minutes after standardized incision following two-hour dark adaptation
scope.comparator: A scalar correction using QE at 500 nm versus correction using measured QE and optical transmission in wavelength bins across 400–870 nm
scope.outcome: Relative error in total photon-emission-rate density and in the estimated 700–870 nm emission fraction

proposed_experiment: Record injured-leaf emission with a calibrated imaging spectrograph or contiguous bandpass filters, determine end-to-end response at each wavelength using a low-flux source, and process the identical raw observations with scalar and wavelength-resolved corrections.

rationale.step: Wound-induced Arabidopsis emission is spectrally nonuniform and is dominated by 700–750 nm, with additional emission reported from 750–870 nm.

cited_works.title: Biophotons and Emergence of Quantum Coherence—A Diffusion Entropy Analysis
cited_works.abstract: We study the emission of photons from germinating seeds using an experimental technique designed to detect light of extremely small intensity. We analyze the dark count signal without germinating seeds as well as the photon emission during the germination process. The technique of analysis adopted here, called diffusion entropy analysis (DEA) and originally designed to measure the temporal complexity of astrophysical, sociological and physiological processes, rests on Kolmogorov complexity. The updated version of DEA used in this paper is designed to determine if the signal complexity is generated either by non-ergodic crucial events with a non-stationary correlation function or by the infinite memory of a stationary but non-integrable correlation function or by a mixture of both processes. We find that dark count yields the ordinary scaling, thereby showing that no complexity of either kinds may occur without any seeds in the chamber. In the presence of seeds in the chamber anomalous scaling emerges, reminiscent of that found in neuro-physiological processes. However, this is a mixture of both processes and with the progress of germination the non-ergodic component tends to vanish and complexity becomes dominated by the stationary infinite memory. We illustrate some conjectures ranging from stress induced annihilation of crucial events to the emergence of quantum coherence.

cited_works.abstract: Cells emit light at ultra-low intensities: photons which are produced as by-products of cellular metabolism, distinct from other light emission processes such as delayed luminescence, bioluminescence, and chemiluminescence. The phenomenon is known by a large range of names, including, but not limited to, biophotons, biological autoluminescence, metabolic photon emission and ultraweak photon emission (UPE), the latter of which shall be used for the purposes of this review. It is worth noting that the photons when produced are neither 'weak' nor specifically biological in characteristics. In this brief review we will examine the history of UPE research, their proposed mechanism, possible biological role, the detection of the phenomenon, and the potential medical applications.

cited_works.title: Stochastic light concentration from 3D to 2D reveals ultraweak chemi- and bioluminescence
cited_works.abstract: For countless applications in science and technology, light must be concentrated, and concentration is classically achieved with reflective and refractive elements. However, there is so far no efficient way, with a 2D detector, to detect photons produced inside an extended volume with a broad or isotropic angular distribution. Here, with theory and experiment, we propose to stochastically transform and concentrate a volume into a smaller surface, using a high-albedo Ulbricht cavity and a small exit orifice through cavity walls. A 3D gas of photons produced inside the cavity is transformed with a 50% number efficiency into a 2D Lambertian emitting orifice with maximal radiance and a much smaller size. With high-albedo quartz-powder cavity walls ([Formula: see text]), the orifice area is [Formula: see text] times smaller than the walls' area. When coupled to a detectivity-optimized photon-counter ([Formula: see text]) the detection limit is [Formula: see text]. cited_works.abstract: Biophotons are non-thermal and non-bioluminescent ultraweak photon emissions, first hypothesised by Gurwitsch as a regulatory mechanism in cell division, and then experimentally observed in living organisms. Today, two main hypotheses explain their origin: stochastic decay of excited molecules and coherent electromagnetic fields produced in biochemical processes. Recent interest focuses on the role of biophotons in cellular communication and disease monitoring. This study presents the first campaign of biophoton emission measurements from cultured astrocytes and glioblastoma cells, conducted at Fondazione Pisana per la Scienza (FPS) using two ultra-sensitive setups developed in collaboration between the National Laboratories of Frascati (LNF-INFN) and the University of Rome II Tor Vergata. The statistical analyses of the collected data revealed a clear separation between cellular signals and dark noise, confirming the high sensitivity of the apparatus. The Diffusion Entropy Analysis (DEA) was applied to the data to uncover dynamic patterns, revealing anomalous diffusion and long-range memory effects that may be related to intercellular signaling and cellular communication. These findings support the hypothesis that biophoton emissions encode rich information beyond intensity, reflecting metabolic and pathological states. cited_works.title: Ultraweak Photon Emissions as a Non-Invasive, Early-Malignancy Detection Tool: An In Vitro and In Vivo Study
cited_works.abstract: Early detection of cancer improves treatment options and increases survival. Building upon previous demonstrations that ultraweak photon emissions (UPE) could be measured to detect cancers, we designed an early detection protocol to test malignancy in both in vitro and in vivo systems. Photons were measured for 100 s from plates containing ~1 million malignant or non-malignant cells from 13 different types of human and mouse cell lines. Tumor cells displayed increased photon emissions compared to non-malignant cells. Examining the standardized Spectral Power Density (SPD) configurations for flux densities between 0.1 and 25 Hz (Δf = 0.01 Hz) yielded 90% discriminant accuracy. The emission profiles of mice that had been injected with melanoma cells could be differentiated from a non-malignant reference groups as early as 24 h post-injection. The peak SPD associated with photon emissions was ~20 Hz for both malignant cell cultures and mice with growing tumors. These results extend the original suggestion by Takeda and his colleagues (2004) published in this journal concerning the potential diagnostic value of UPEs for assessing proliferations of carcinoma cells. The specificity of the spectral profile in the 20 Hz range may be relevant to the consistent efficacy reported by several authors that weak magnetic field pulsations within this frequency range can diminish the growth of malignant cells in culture and tumor weights in mice.

scope.comparator: Spontaneous (unprovoked) UPE intensity from the identical site, subject, session and detector - a within-subject head-to-head, not a cross-study comparison.
scope.outcome: Area under the ROC curve on the held-out set, evaluated once, for each of the two locked classifiers.

null_hypothesis: Delta-AUC (provoked minus spontaneous) is <= 0, or its upper 95% CI bound lies below 0.10 - i.e. provocation buys no discriminative advantage over the spontaneous intensity on which nearly all existing clinical UPE claims rest.

proposed_experiment: Pre-registered two-arm diagnostic accuracy study. rationale.step: A within-study dissociation between spontaneous and provoked UPE already exists in the corpus: in erythropoietic protoporphyria patients, spontaneous UPE resembled that of healthy individuals, while the post-solar-simulated-light initial burst correlated with plasma iron and erythrocyte protoporphyrin IX and was suppressed by oral zinc. Spontaneous emission carried no disease information; provoked emission did.

UVA-provoked UPE is the only human UPE readout in the corpus that has been shown to move dose-dependently with a controlled intervention in formal clinical trials (two trials, 20 volunteers each, dose-dependent antioxidant effect of topical vitamin C and alpha-glucosylrutin), and the same work qualifies UVA-provoked UPE explicitly as a validated non-invasive method.

Spontaneous human skin UPE is on the order of tens to hundreds of photons per second per square centimetre, whereas UV provocation raises skin emission by a factor that scales with UV dose and is suppressible by antioxidants - i.e. the provoked signal sits far above the spontaneous one on the same detector.

Photon-shot-noise calculation of the SNR gain: take spontaneous emission s = 10 detected counts/s (100 photons/s/cm2 over 1 cm2 at ~10% end-to-end detection efficiency) against a background b = 10 counts/s, integrated for T = 100 s. SNR = sT/sqrt((s+b)T) = 1000/sqrt(2000) = 22.4. A provocation that raises the emission tenfold gives s = 100 counts/s: SNR = 10000/sqrt(11000) = 95.3. The provoked acquisition delivers a ~4.3-fold SNR gain at fixed integration time, which for a fixed true group separation propagates directly into higher attainable discrimination.

The field's own analytical review recommends populations of approximately 50-100 subjects for human UPE studies, so the n >= 100 per arm specified here is the smallest sample the field itself would accept as adequate.

cited_works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is a rare, inherited disorder of haem biosynthesis owing to deficient ferrochelatase (FECH) and accumulation of protoporphyrin IX (PPIX). This results in acute cutaneous photosensitivity upon light exposure with production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and ultra-weak photon emission (UPE) as a by-product. We investigated if UPE evaluated the light sensitivity in EPP patients and influence of zinc treatment. METHODS: Fourteen EPP patients took zinc sulphate (3 × 200 mg/day) during spring and summer. Using a photomultiplier (PM), UPE was measured from the buttock skin and dorsal hand before and after solar-simulated light (SUN) exposure. Blood samples were analysed routinely for plasma zinc, iron, ferritin, transferrin, haemoglobin, erythrocyte PPIX and Zn-PPIX. RESULTS: UPE in EPP patients resembled that seen in healthy individuals. Without treatment, a seasonal decrease was seen from spring to summer in four control patients. However, oral zinc treatment reduced ROS formation significantly regardless of SUN exposure. After SUN exposure, the initial burst was correlated to plasma iron and erythrocyte PPIX. During treatment, an inverse correlation was found between plasma zinc concentration and the initial burst. CONCLUSION: Measurements of UPE can be used for monitoring UVA-induced oxidative processes in vivo in the skin of EPP patients.
